tasks.title: Ship 3 librarian agents + MCP servers: self-updating project indexes, selectable in /init-team, wired to the lanes that consult them
notes: USER: deferred by request ('later once you finish'). Queued behind T8.

REFERENCE PATTERN (read from '/home/ubuntu/source/Appnext Campaign AI/campaign-ai-platform/.claude/agents'): _librarian-template.md (canonical, 190 lines), history-librarian.md, tests-librarian.md, compliance-officer.md (55KB). Shape of each: haiku model; tools Glob/Grep/Read/Bash/Write/Edit; owns a private memory dir .claude/agent-memory/<name>/ holding an append-only commits.jsonl plus rolling summary_overall.md and summary_by_file.md; SELF-UPDATES incrementally on every invocation (e.g. git log since the last indexed hash); answers FROM memory via a bash search helper so the caller never pays for raw git output; explicitly does not touch production code, bump versions or push. Descriptions carry 2-3 <example> blocks so the orchestrator auto-delegates. Librarians consult each other (compliance-officer consults tests-librarian).
GOAL: teamme maps the project once via librarians instead of every generated agent re-deriving the same map its own way. The librarians are the project-comprehension layer, not roster filler.

OPEN DESIGN QUESTIONS for the future brief: (1) 'gate' needs defining - MCP tool-level refusal like teamme_install (precedent now exists in T8) vs a hook, which invariant #1 forbids from blocking; (2) 'self-updated autonomously with hooks' needs a trigger that cannot loop (invariant #2) and cannot block (invariant #1) - SessionStart is the safe candidate, PostToolUse is not; (3) which 3 - the reference set is git-history, tests-coverage and compliance, but teamme's own layer boundaries may imply different ones; (4) a librarian's memory is per-project state: committed or gitignored? (5) invariant #4 - librarian prompts are project-agnostic templates, their INDEXES are project-specific.

HISTORY-LIBRARIAN SCOPE (user, for the future brief): go beyond answering 'what changed in file X'. Two capabilities: (1) build a codebase MAP from historical changes read chronologically - the commit stream is the evidence, so structure emerges from how the code actually evolved rather than from a one-off static scan; (2) print a COMPLETE DEPENDENCY TREE of anything - workflow -> references -> scopes -> features -> tests, with the tests leg answered by consulting the tests-librarian rather than re-deriving it. That cross-librarian consultation is the pattern already present in the reference implementation (compliance-officer consults tests-librarian) and is what makes the map cheap: each librarian owns one axis and is asked, never re-computed.
Related: T27 (cross-project grants) may be the access-control layer this needs - librarian indexes are the obvious cross-project payload.

STORAGE DECISION (user's steer): back the librarian indexes with sqlite3, which is in the PYTHON STANDARD LIBRARY (3.45.1 on this machine) - so a real indexed DB costs no dependency and invariant #3 still holds. This is a material upgrade on the reference implementation's append-only jsonl + bash grep helper: it makes the indexes queryable rather than searchable. The dependency tree the user asked for (workflow -> references -> scopes -> features -> tests) is a recursive CTE, which SQLite does natively; jsonl cannot express it without rebuilding a graph in memory each time.

SCOPE CORRECTION: indexing needs NO cross-project identity. A librarian's DB lives inside the project (.claude/agent-memory/ or beside it) and is isolated positionally, exactly like worklog.json. The identity problem I raised applies only to T27 (sharing across projects), not to building the indexes.

WHAT TO INDEX (user): code, git history, bugs. Natural tables - commits (hash, author, date, scope tag), files_changed (commit -> path), symbols/imports/references (the dependency graph), tests (test -> source edges, coverage gaps), and the work log's own tasks, which already exist and could join to the files a task touched. The MCP server is the natural owner of the connection: it already runs as a process holding the project path, so it can expose query tools instead of every agent shelling out to grep.

HONEST GAP IN MY GROUNDING: I read _librarian-template.md and the headers of history-librarian.md and tests-librarian.md, but NOT compliance-officer.md (55KB) in full. The future brief must read it properly - it is the largest of the four and the one that shows how a librarian is consulted BY another agent rather than invoked directly.

FULL SPEC (user, verbatim intent): teamme provides OUT-OF-THE-BOX native indexing via a local DB owned by the MCP server. Capabilities: codebase mapping; a workflow expert; links between every aspect of the project; mapping existing tests to code, components and features; reported bugs too if an issue-tracking librarian is enabled; and a TREE MAP OF GIT HISTORY driven by reasoning about what actually happened in each commit - so any aspect of the development is easy to query, related changes are visible, and commit messages act as a STORYTELLING tool giving precise understanding of when, what and WHY a change was made. Self-refreshed on each plan before it is marked resolved, via hooks acting as gates that enforce committing the refreshed indexes along with the change.

STORAGE FORK (user): make it selectable whether the librarians' data is committed with the code or lives alongside it uncommitted. Applies to ALL generated knowledge - librarian indexes, the MCP server's knowledge base, and the agents' memories - not just one of them.

DESIGN TENSION 1 - a SQLite file cannot be committed sanely. It is binary, so git cannot merge it: two teammates indexing different commits produce divergent files that conflict irreconcilably, and every reindex churns the whole blob. This is probably WHY the reference implementation chose append-only commits.jsonl plus rolling markdown summaries - those merge. Likely resolution: keep the COMMITTED artifact append-only text (jsonl/markdown) and treat SQLite as a locally-rebuilt query layer derived from it. That satisfies both halves of the user's fork: committed-with-code means the text artifacts, uncommitted means gitignore them and rebuild locally. Do not commit the .db.

DESIGN TENSION 2 - 'hooks acting as gates that enforce committing' vs invariant #1: invariant #1 governs the WRITE GUARD (PreToolUse must fail open). A Stop hook that refuses to end a turn is a different, already-sanctioned mechanism - worklog-enforce.py stop already blocks on an active task. So an index-freshness gate belongs on Stop, not PreToolUse, and must obey invariant #2: state what re-arms it or it traps the session. The T10 lesson applies directly - stamp against a status-change field, never a mutation timestamp, or refreshing the index re-arms the nag that demanded the refresh.

tasks.title: Cross-project shared knowledge: explicit per-project grants with read-only vs write, over the MCP server
notes: USER'S IDEA: teamme's MCP server could hold data across projects as shared knowledge, but only for projects the user explicitly grants, and with read-only vs write chosen per grant.

GROUNDING - the capability already exists, unscoped: teamme_mcp.py:133 takes project_dir from tool args (falling back to CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR then cwd) with NO validation, so teamme_worklog can already read and write any project's ledger on disk. Not a privilege escalation - the server runs as the user and the agent has Bash anyway - but undirected: nothing scopes it, nothing records consent, nothing reports afterwards that another project was touched. So the work is constraining and curating an existing capability, not adding one.

DESIGN QUESTIONS for the brief: (1) where do grants live? Per-project (.claude/) means a project declares who may read IT, which is the right direction for consent, but the server must then read the target's grant file, not the caller's. (2) Read-only vs write is only meaningful if the server enforces it - a prompt-level rule is not a permission. (3) What is actually shared? The work log is project-specific and low value cross-project; the interesting payload is closer to T14's librarian indexes. Consider whether T27 is the transport layer for T14 rather than a separate feature. (4) Revocation and staleness: a grant to a project that no longer exists, or was renamed. (5) An explicit deny-by-default, since today's behaviour is allow-everything.

tasks.title: Session librarian: index every session turn as it happens, so context lost to compaction can be fetched back by mark point instead of re-reading the transcript
notes: USER SPEC, verbatim intent: 'add auto-compaction session indexing as a librarian which can go back and fetch context from any session before compaction happened, and get it after compaction. by without requiring to read all the session, by indexing all the parts of a session (chat history) and store mark points in db. then there won't be any need to tell you to prepare for compaction, every step in a session will be indexed and added to the db of the plugin's mcp server.' The goal is explicit and testable: after a compaction, a question whose answer exists only in the pre-compaction region should resolve from the index, without re-reading the transcript.

GROUNDING, verified this session: session transcripts are real files on disk, one JSONL per session, under a per-project slug directory - this session is ~/.claude-personal/projects/-home-ubuntu-source-teamme/87e18ef7-....jsonl, and the conventional location ~/.claude/projects/<slug>/ also exists on this box with entries for other repos. JSONL is append-only, so indexing is incremental by byte offset: the indexer never re-reads what it already consumed. That is what makes 'index every step' affordable, and it is the same incremental property T14 needs for the code index.

VERIFIED, not assumed: the installed CLI (2.1.281) contains the hook event names PreCompact, SessionEnd, SubagentStop and PostToolUse alongside the four teamme already uses (grep -ao against /home/ubuntu/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.281: PreCompact 39 hits, SessionEnd 54, SubagentStop 56, PostToolUse 189). So a compaction boundary IS observable to a hook. Confirm the payload shape and the settings key against the docs before wiring it - presence of the string proves the event exists, not what it hands the script.

DESIGN, the load-bearing decision: indexing must be CONTINUOUS, and PreCompact must be only a boundary MARKER, never the indexer's trigger. Indexing at PreCompact would just relocate 'prepare for compaction' into a hook - same single point of failure, now invisible: one slow or failed run and the entire window is gone precisely when it can no longer be recovered. Continuous is also the only shape that matches the user's words, 'every step in a session will be indexed'. The tick can come from hooks teamme already owns (UserPromptSubmit, Stop) plus SessionEnd for a final flush; each run only consumes bytes appended since the last offset. PreCompact then writes one row saying 'everything before here is no longer in context', which is exactly the mark point retrieval needs to answer 'what did we lose'.

TENSION 1, storage: this is the one librarian whose index must NEVER be committable. T14 offers a choice - commit the librarians' knowledgebase alongside the code, or keep it beside the repo. For the session index that choice must not exist. A transcript contains everything anyone typed into the session, including secrets pasted in by accident, and indexing it creates a second copy that outlives the paste-cache. It lives machine-local, gitignored, with no cross-project grant under T27 unless the user asks for that specifically and separately. Also worth deciding: a retention bound, since an unbounded index of every session on the machine grows forever.

TENSION 2, the retrieval contract is the whole feature and the easiest part to get wrong: a fetch must return a BOUNDED slice. A tool that answers 'what did we decide about X before compaction' by handing back 40k tokens of transcript has reproduced the problem it exists to solve - it just moved the cost from re-reading the file to re-reading the reply. The index needs to store enough per mark point (turn boundary, tool call, file written, task status transition, compaction boundary) to answer WHERE something was discussed, so the fetch can be a targeted range and not a dump. Define what a mark point is before writing any schema - that definition IS the design.

RELATION to T14: same machinery (plugin-shipped, enabled/disabled at plugin level, not roster-selectable, SQLite from the stdlib, consulted by team agents), different source class. The other three librarians index the repo - versioned, shareable, reconstructible from git. This one indexes the conversation - unversioned, private, machine-local, and gone if not captured as it happens. That asymmetry is why it is a separate task rather than a fourth bullet on T14, and why its storage answer differs from theirs.

DESIGN CORRECTION, and it overturns my own earlier note on this task. I wrote that indexing must be CONTINUOUS and that PreCompact must only be a marker, because indexing at compaction time would be a single point of failure. The first half is now wrong: nothing needs to be captured in flight, because THE HARNESS ALREADY WRITES EVERYTHING. Measured on this live session: ~/.claude-personal/projects/<slug>/<session>.jsonl is 8.7 MB and 3,843 lines, append-only, containing assistant/user/attachment/system/tool records AND compaction events (61 hits for 'compact'). It survives compaction because it is a file, not context. CONSEQUENCE: indexing can be LAZY - run it when someone asks, read only the bytes appended since the last offset, exactly as the git indexer does. That means ZERO new hooks, no per-turn latency, and nothing joining REQUIRED_HOOKS. The same trick as phase 1: the indexer lives in the plugin and is invoked by the MCP server, so nothing is copied into a project. PreCompact remains OPTIONAL and additive, not required - the transcript appears to record compaction itself, so the boundary may be derivable without any hook at all. Verify that before building anything that depends on a hook.

PRIVACY IS ENFORCED THE WAY index.db ALREADY IS, not by documentation. A transcript holds everything anyone typed, including secrets pasted by accident, and an index of it is a second copy. So the session store goes in the project at .claude/librarians/sessions/ - preserving teamme's positional isolation, no cross-project identity needed (that is T27's problem, not this one) - and is written into the SAME marked .gitignore block as index.db, where it is NEVER A CHOICE. commit_record must not apply to it. This keeps one mechanism instead of inventing a second, and the phase 2 rule still holds: teamme never removes an ignore line it did not write.

SUBSTRATE BUILT, and note 8 is confirmed by measurement rather than assumed. COMPACTION IS DERIVABLE WITHOUT ANY HOOK: the transcript carries type=system / subtype=compact_boundary with full compactMetadata (trigger, preTokens 596182 -> postTokens 17958, cumulativeDroppedTokens 578224, preservedSegment uuids), followed by a user record with isCompactSummary=true. No PreCompact hook is involved and none is needed; nothing joins REQUIRED_HOOKS. Two new modules in plugins/teamme/server/librarian/: transcripts.py (the ENTIRE harness-layout assumption - where the files are and what a line in one looks like - between one banner comment and the next, read live, degrading to a cwd-based scan and then to an honest 'not found') and sessions.py (schema, incremental byte-offset indexer, four bounded queries). MARK POINT, the definition the schema follows from: a position a person could later point at and name - prompt / message / recap / answer / tool / file / compaction - hanging off TURNS, one content-bearing record each, numbered seq per session, stable because the file is append-only. MEASURED on this repo's own transcripts: cold 35.6 MB across 47 files -> 2,789 turns, 2,790 marks in 0.51s; a no-op incremental refresh 0.11s reading 0 bytes; 400 KB of genuinely new bytes 0.16s. Index 2.98 MB, 8.4% of source. Worst-case query payload ~24k characters (~6k tokens) against an 8.7 MB file. DISCOVERY THE BRIEF DID NOT COVER: subagent threads live in a separate sidecar tree, <session-id>/subagents/agent-*.jsonl, 26 MB against the main thread's 8.7 MB on this session - on a team that dispatches specialists, most of the reasoning a later question asks about happened there. Each is its own append-only file, so each is indexed as a child session row (parent_session, agent from the .meta.json) with no change to the model. BUG FOUND AND FIXED while testing: a record larger than MAX_LINE_BYTES came back from readline() without a newline and was mistaken for a live tail, parking the byte offset in front of it forever - one huge record would have wedged a session's index permanently. Now distinguished by whether the read hit the size cap or EOF. PRIVACY: .claude/librarians/sessions/ is written into config.py's ALWAYS_IGNORED set beside index.db, so commit_record cannot reach it; verified commit_record=true still ignores the directory. No JSONL record, deliberately: the transcript IS the record and a second text copy of a conversation doubles a private surface for nothing.

All watch-fails performed on throwaway cp -r scratch copies of plugins/teamme/server under the scratchpad dir, never the real tree, then deleted. Suite runtime 8.4s -> ~9.0s. Ran validate.sh twice end to end, exit 0 both times, ALL CHECKS PASSED. No code under plugins/teamme/server/librarian/ was changed - the code was correct, only scripts/validate.sh gained coverage.

RELEASE LANE closed after one correction. The first draft named three session queries that DO NOT EXIST (recent/search/compactions instead of sessions/search_turns/compaction) plus a 'sessions-librarian' tool that was never built. validate.sh passed anyway - nothing compares documented identifiers to code, which is now T37. I REPEATED THE MISTAKE I HAD JUST RECORDED. The docs lane found that NO prompt mentions the session queries - verified, zero occurrences of search_turns/compaction/sessions across history-librarian.md, init-team.md and templates/intake.md. So the four queries are live and reachable only by an agent that already knows they exist. This is exactly the commit_detail miss from 0.4.0, and T34's note already says why it happens: 'adding a tool to the server is only half of shipping it when the consumer is a prompt - a server-lane change that a prompt must know about needs the prompt lane in the same phase, or the feature is inert.' tasks.title: Librarian substrate (T14 phase 1): SQLite store rebuildable from append-only text, incremental git indexer, and MCP query tools - no agents, no gate, nothing copied into projects
notes: Parent: T14 (umbrella, stays open). Phases 2-5 remain specified-not-dispatched in T14's notes; T30 is the session librarian. READ T14's notes 20-25 before starting - they carry the reference-implementation findings, the harness constraint on plugin agents, and the architecture the user approved this session.

BUILT (phase 1 substrate, uncommitted): plugins/teamme/server/librarian/{__init__,store,history}.py plus three MCP tools (teamme_librarian_status/refresh/query) in teamme_mcp.py, and .gitignore entries for the derived index. Nothing copied into a target project, nothing added to REQUIRED_HOOKS - the indexer runs inside the MCP server, so T23's growing-list trap is avoided by construction.

MEASURED (in-process, so interpreter start is excluded). This repo, 10 commits/122 file rows: cold full index 0.137s, warm refresh 0.010s, rebuild-from-text 0.045s, queries 0.03-0.10ms. A 10,393-commit repo (local clone of vllm, 52,947 file rows): cold 15.0s ONCE, incremental +50 commits 0.40s (~8ms/commit), warm refresh with nothing new 0.012s, rebuild-from-text 1.26s, commits_touching 9-11ms, recent 0.09ms. Artifacts at that scale: commits.jsonl 9.0 MiB, index.db 22 MiB. VERDICT: phases 2-5 proceed as designed - a per-turn refresh costs ~12ms when idle, which is well inside preflight's budget.

CONTRADICTS T21's premise: python3 -c pass measured 23-42ms today on this machine (7 runs), not ~1.1s. sqlite3 import 43ms, importing the librarian package 56ms. Whatever T21 hit was not reproducible today - worth re-checking before any other decision leans on that figure.

PROVEN by hand, not yet by validate.sh: rebuild-from-text (db deleted, rebuilt, commits/files_changed/commit_parents rows and the marker byte-identical, at both scales); unreachable marker after a force-push falls back to full AND says so; empty repo = success with zero rows; not-a-git-repo and git-missing = clean error payload; malformed JSONL line skipped not fatal; CORRUPT index.db is discarded and rebuilt rather than raising; 10 concurrent refreshes leave no lock/tmp debris and no duplicate rows; a race while 5 commits land writes each commit exactly once; paths with newlines/quotes, non-UTF-8 bytes, binary files (NULL counts), merges (no file rows) and renames all parse. GAP FOR VALIDATION: scripts/validate.sh compiles plugins/*/server/*.py, which does NOT reach server/librarian/*.py.

VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY by the orchestrator, not taken on report: (1) validate.sh passes, exit 0. (2) py_compile clean on all three new files plus teamme_mcp.py. (3) The reported validate.sh gap is REAL - line 45's glob 'plugins/*/server/*.py' expands to teamme_mcp.py only and never reaches server/librarian/*.py. (4) REBUILD-FROM-TEXT re-run from scratch with PATH stripped to /nonexistent so git was genuinely unavailable: db deleted, rebuilt from commits.jsonl alone in 0.038s - 10/10 commits, 122/122 files_changed, 9/9 commit_parents, rows tuple-identical, marker preserved. (5) No truncation: git rev-list --count HEAD == 10 == rows in db, oldest and newest subjects match the real first and last commits. (6) Warm refresh 0.021s. The only expensive operation is the one-time cold index (15s at 10k commits).

tasks.title: Roster defect: agents without Bash cannot use worklog.py, so they edit .claude/intake/worklog.json directly and bypass the lockfile
notes: OBSERVED, not theoretical: during T31 the docs lane (teamme-docs-writer, tools Read/Edit/Write/Grep/Glob - no Bash) appended its note by editing .claude/intake/worklog.json with Edit, concurrently with the orchestrator writing notes through worklog.py's O_EXCL lock. It happened to survive - valid JSON, 31 tasks, all notes intact, no debris - but that is luck. The lock exists precisely because 3 of 24 notes were measurably lost before it was added. Two agents in the shipped roster template have no Bash, so they have no correct option: the ledger is the one file every lane must write and the only writer is a CLI. FIXES WORTH WEIGHING: (a) give every generated agent Bash scoped to worklog.py, (b) expose the worklog over the MCP server so a Bash-less agent can write it safely - teamme_worklog ALREADY EXISTS and does exactly this, so the real gap may just be that generated agents are never told to use it, (c) have the orchestrator record notes on the lane's behalf. (b) looks strongest and nearly free. Same defect class as the prompt-author lane being unable to git mv.

A THIRD failure mode for writing the ledger, distinct from the no-Bash one this task already records: writing a note THROUGH bash silently corrupts any backticked identifier, because the shell substitutes it as a command. It happened to me just now on T37 - the note recorded with its identifiers missing and no error, and only a re-read caught it. bash printed "configure: command not found" to stderr, which is easy to miss in a long output. The ledger is append-only, so a corrupted note cannot be repaired, only superseded. Relevant to this task because the proposed fix - route notes through the teamme_worklog MCP tool instead of the worklog.py CLI - removes the shell from the path entirely and fixes all three failure modes at once: no-Bash agents can write, the lockfile is respected, and no shell metacharacter can eat content.

tasks.title: Librarian tier (T14 phase 2): ship the first plugin-shipped agent - a history librarian - plus the per-project enable/disable mechanism, the consultation contract team agents follow, and the storage fork
notes: SCOPE, and why it is one librarian and not three: phase 1 built ONE index (history). Shipping a tests-librarian or code-librarian agent now would be a prompt with nothing behind it - an agent that can only say 'I have no data'. Phase 2 therefore ships the HISTORY librarian only, and with it the whole tier mechanism (plugin-shipped agents/, per-project enable/disable, the consultation contract, the storage fork). Phase 3 then adds each further librarian as index+agent together, which the mechanism makes cheap. This also means phase 2 delivers the user's storytelling capability WITHOUT any new indexing: the agent reads commits from the existing index and reasons at query time. Stored reasoned enrichment (the 'kind' seam store.py already preserves through a full reindex) is an optimization, not a prerequisite - defer it.

MECHANISM DECIDED (orchestrator's call, routine): (1) CONFIG lives at .claude/librarians/config.json, per project, owned by the MCP server - which also sidesteps T32, since a Bash-less agent can reach it through a tool instead of editing a file. (2) DISABLED cannot mean absent: a plugin-shipped agent is visible in every project once the plugin is installed and cannot be hidden per-project. So disabled means the librarian tools REFUSE for that librarian, naming how to enable it, and the agent prompt checks status first - the same shape as the existing teamme_install gate, which is honest about being a refusal rather than a harness guarantee. (3) STORAGE FORK is a config key, not a doc instruction: commit_record true|false, defaulting to FALSE (do not commit). teamme writes or removes the .gitignore entry for commits.jsonl to match, so the choice is enacted rather than merely recorded. Default false because until the phase-4 freshness gate exists, a committed index only goes stale on every commit that does not refresh it - the reason this repo's own record was untracked in 5ea3e23.

PROMPT SIDE LANDED (note recorded by the orchestrator - the prompt lane has no Bash, which is T32 again): plugins/teamme/agents/history-librarian.md is teamme's first plugin-shipped agent - query-only, model sonnet (deliberately not the reference's haiku, because the mechanical extraction is already done by server/librarian/ and what is left for the agent IS the reasoning), no permissionMode/hooks/mcpServers per the verified plugin-agent constraint, memory omitted because the enum is computed in the CLI bundle and cannot be read by grep - and because the agent persists nothing anyway. tasks.title: Librarian phase 3: a code librarian whose edges come from co-change in the commit stream, not from parsing source - plus a tests librarian on the same signal
notes: THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES PHASE 3: the user asked for a complete dependency tree - 'workflow -> references -> scopes -> features -> tests'. The obvious implementation is static parsing, and it is the wrong one here. teamme is python3-stdlib-only (invariant #3) and project-agnostic (invariant #4), so a static index would need a parser per language, shipped with no dependencies, and would silently degrade to nothing on any stack nobody wrote a parser for - the same 'indistinguishable from not working' failure invariant #3 exists to prevent.

THE ANSWER IS ALREADY IN T14'S NOTES, in the user's own words: 'build a codebase MAP from historical changes read chronologically - the commit stream is the evidence, so structure emerges from how the code actually evolved rather than from a one-off static scan.' That is CO-CHANGE COUPLING: files that change together in the same commit are related, and the strength of the edge is how often. It needs NO parsing, works on every language including config and docs, and runs entirely off the files_changed table phase 1 already built - so the code librarian costs a query layer, not a new indexer. It also captures edges static analysis misses: a schema and the migration that follows it, a feature and its docs, a constant and the config that mirrors it. The tests librarian rides the same signal - a test file that keeps changing alongside a source file IS the test-to-code edge, language-agnostic. Static parsing stays available as a LATER, optional enrichment layer for one language at a time; it is not the foundation.

HONEST LIMITS to state in the brief and the docs, because co-change is evidence and not proof: (1) it finds correlation, not a call graph - two files that always change together may share a cause rather than a dependency, and the librarian must say 'changes with' not 'depends on'. (2) It is blind to a real dependency that never changed - stable code has no edges. (3) A giant mechanical commit (a reformat, a license header, a rename sweep) couples everything it touched, so edges need a commit-size cutoff or a weighting that damps them. (4) A shallow or young repo has little signal, which history.probe()'s shallow flag can already report. Every one of these argues for reporting an edge WITH its evidence - N commits, most recent SHA - rather than as a bare assertion.

PHASE 2 VALIDATED BY USE before phase 3 was dispatched. Consulted the live history-librarian on two real questions about this repo. It detected the index was behind HEAD, refreshed, and SAID SO; cited a SHA for every claim; read the commit stream chronologically and recovered the reasoning from commit bodies; and closed with a 'not covered' section naming what the index cannot answer. I spot-checked its citations against git rather than trusting them: 78b54d6 does introduce the installed_plugins.json rung (4 hits in that commit's diff), 2ebb889 is where hook_freshness() is defined (+1 def), and its claim that NO commit in the repo touches only scripts/validate.sh holds when checked across all 15 commits. It is reading the index and reasoning over it, not confabulating.

Server side shipped: three co-change queries in store.py (changes_with, coupling_between, hotspots) plus their renderers and schema in teamme_mcp.py. No new tables, no new index pass - all three read the files_changed rows phase 1 already writes. Damping: a commit touching more than DEFAULT_MAX_COMMIT_FILES=25 files is treated as a sweep and excluded from every edge count, overridable per call with max_files; every answer prints considered/skipped/indexed counts, so the largest input to the ranking is visible. coupling_between deliberately does NOT damp its listing - it exists to inspect an edge, so it lists every shared commit and marks the too-broad ones. Vocabulary is 'changes with' throughout; the three honest limits (correlation not a call graph, stable code has no edges, one shared commit is weak) print as caveats on every result, and a shallow clone adds a fourth from history.probe().

Verified, not assumed: changes_with and hotspots on this repo were compared row-for-row against ground truth read straight from 'git log --name-only' with the librarian module out of the loop - anchor count, partner counts, every shared count and the skipped-as-broad count all matched. changes_with on templates/hooks/preflight.py puts .claude/hooks/preflight.py first (overlap 1.0) and scripts/validate.sh in the top tied group, as expected. A fixture with three 35-file sweeps shows damping working in both directions: default cap leaves a.py with exactly one partner (a_test.py), max_files=100 floods the ranking with 30 unrelated junk files at 3 shared commits each. Empty repo, one-commit repo, shallow clone, a path whose every commit was damped away, a path with no partners at all, an unknown path, and malformed max_files (bool/float/list/negative/string) all return payloads - nothing raised, exit 0, empty stderr. ./scripts/validate.sh passes. NOT done: validate.sh has no section for these queries yet, and agents/history-librarian.md + README still document only the six phase-1 queries.

SCOPE CALL: there will be NO separate 'code librarian' agent. The co-change queries are a HISTORY signal - they read the same commit stream, from the same index, and cite the same SHAs. A second agent querying the same source of truth would be duplication with a different name, and would split 'ask about history' across two places for no gain. history-librarian absorbs changes_with / coupling_between / hotspots instead. A genuinely separate code librarian would be one doing STATIC analysis - a different evidence base entirely - and that is not what phase 3 built. Consequence: T34's title ('a code librarian... plus a tests librarian') is imprecise, like T14's before it. T28 (no retitle action in worklog.py) is why this is a note and not a fix.

SERVER SIDE VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY against git, not taken on report: git says the preflight template and its in-repo copy share all 5 commits, and template<->validate.sh also 5. The tool reports 4 for each and states why - '4 considered commit(s) (5 in the index before damping)' - because d767f28 touched 28 files and exceeded the 25-file sweep cap. Jaccard checks out: 4/4 = 1.0 for the copy (they change together and almost nothing else), 4/(4+7-4) = 0.571 for validate.sh. The believability test set in the brief PASSED: validate.sh is in the top tied group, which it had to be, since every commit touching preflight also touched the suite. Output header reads 'correlation, not a call graph' - the vocabulary rule is in the tool output, not just the docs.

PROMPT SIDE landed (recorded by the orchestrator - no Bash in that lane, T32 again). history-librarian.md 150 -> 258 lines, 5 examples, no forbidden frontmatter keys, validate.sh exit 0 (and that pass now means something: phase 2's agent-frontmatter check is what validates it). All nine queries documented, a new step 3 making 'changes with' a vocabulary rule with a four-row limits table, a co-change walk (hotspots -> changes_with -> coupling_between -> commit_detail), a mandatory 'basis:' line in the output contract, and two new refusals covering dependency/import/call graphs.

PHASE 2 MISS FOUND BY PHASE 3, worth remembering: commit_detail was NEVER documented in history-librarian.md. We shipped the query in 0.4.0 specifically so the agent would stop grepping raw JSONL for commit bodies - and the prompt still told it to grep. The tool existed, the prompt did not know, so the capability was shipped and unused. LESSON: adding a tool to the server is only half of shipping it when the consumer is a prompt. A server-lane change that a prompt must know about needs the prompt lane in the same phase, or the feature is inert. Nothing in validate.sh could have caught this - it is a prompt-to-tool coupling, and there is no eval suite.

THE PROMPT LANE'S OWN REASONING, worth keeping: on why the rule belongs in the prompt when the tool already prints it - 'a caveat on the input cannot govern your prose, and prose is where the weaker claim quietly becomes the stronger one.' And on tests - it says 'these tests change with this code', never 'these tests cover this code', because 'coverage is a claim about what executes; the index has no execution in it.' That is the correct line and it should survive into the docs. It also reported four honest prompt-to-renderer mismatches rather than papering over them: the tool emits prose, not the named row fields; share_of_anchor is computed and never rendered; the overlap tie-break is invisible in output so the prompt claims only 'most shared first'; and 'weak' means one SHARED commit in changes_with but one commit total in hotspots.

validate.sh: added 4 co-change assertions (changes_with vs git-log ground truth with the module out of the loop; damping in both directions with counts; coupling_between marking a too-broad shared commit rather than hiding it; the 4 distinguishable empty/annotated changes_with payloads - unknown/damped-away/alone/young). All 4 watched failing first via targeted, reverted sed breaks in store.py (off-by-one shared_commits, a neutralized broad-commit threshold, an ignored max_files override, an always-False too_broad flag, a collapsed empty_reason branch), then confirmed passing after restore (store.py byte-identical to pre-experiment state, verified with diff). Suite: 13.0s before (stashed) -> 14.3s after, exit 0 both times. Closes the gap 'the commits_touching, commits_between and search_subjects query variants... none has a validate.sh section' for the new co-change layer specifically. Still open: commits_touching/commits_between/search_subjects themselves remain unasserted directly; hotspots has no validate.sh coverage at all (only changes_with and coupling_between got assertions here, per the brief's scope); teamme_librarian_configure's MCP-level co-change rendering (_render_cochange in teamme_mcp.py) is exercised only indirectly through store.query, not over the JSON-RPC pipe.

VALIDATION LANE landed and verified independently: 45 sections (was 41), exit 0, 15.4s (was ~13s pre-lane). Four watch-fail proofs, each broken and seen failing: shared_commits off by one (caught by ground truth parsed from git log with the module out of the loop), the damping cap raised to 25000 AND _breadth ignoring max_files (both directions, so the cap is proven to be doing the work rather than the fixture being thin), too_broad forced False, and the damped-away empty message collapsed into the unknown-path one. I checked the reverts held rather than trusting them: DEFAULT_MAX_COMMIT_FILES is 25, zero occurrences of 'COUNT(*) - 1', zero of 'raw = None'. Follow-ups queued as T35 (untested renderers, and hotspots unasserted).

RELEASE LANE closed: 0.4.0 -> 0.5.0, marketplace re-verified as carrying no version, CHANGELOG 0.5.0 entry written. Sent back once: the first draft omitted two limits the brief asked for and the lane had marked one 'implicit in correlation'. It is not implicit, and it is the dangerous one - an empty changes_with result on a file nobody has touched in a year reads as 'nothing uses this' unless the entry says otherwise, and someone acts on that by deleting or refactoring freely. Same shape as T23 and T26: a confidently wrong answer is worse than an honest 'no evidence', and an empty co-change result IS an 'I don't know' that must read like one. Both limits are now stated plainly in the Added bullet, which is where a reader forms their expectation of what the feature can tell them.

DOCS LANE landed and verified (recorded by the orchestrator - no Bash in that lane). It corrected TWO things rather than transcribing: (1) it read the real validate.sh fixture and found MY worklog note wrong - I had recorded 'three 35-file sweeps / max_files=100' from the hook lane's own manual fixture, but the shipped assertion uses one 30-file sweep and max_files=40. It documented the code, not my note, which is the right order of authority. (2) It found CLAUDE.md's 'history-librarian.md is unvalidated' gap entry STALE and rewrote it. That staleness is MY miss: in phase 2 I told the docs lane to write nothing about validate.sh coverage and said I would add the prose myself once validation landed - I verified the coverage and never updated the gap entry. The entry now correctly narrows the gap to 'frontmatter is validated; what it instructs is not'.

tasks.title: Watch-fail briefs must say HOW to break the code when it lives in another lane's file
notes: MY BRIEF DEFECT, caught by a near-miss during T35. I told the validation lane 'watch it fail' AND 'only scripts/validate.sh' in the same brief. tasks.title: validate.sh does not check that identifiers named in CHANGELOG/README exist in the code - a doc can name a query that does not exist and CI stays green
notes: CAUGHT LIVE during the 0.6.0 release: the changelog entry named three session queries that do not exist - 'recent' (really 'sessions'), 'search' (really 'search_turns') and 'compactions' (really 'compaction') - plus a 'sessions-librarian' tool that was never added. validate.sh passed anyway, because nothing compares documented identifiers against the code. A user copying {"query":"search"} out of the changelog gets 'unknown session query'. That is worse than an undocumented feature: documentation that fails when followed. CHEAP FIX, and it fits this repo's existing discipline: extract every backticked identifier from CHANGELOG.md and both READMEs that looks like a query or tool name, and assert it appears in the corresponding QUERY_NAMES tuple or tool registry. Same shape as the manifests check that now walks the plugin tree - a mechanical check for a class of error a human reviewer reliably misses.

PROTOTYPE, already proven against the real 0.6.0 entry - this is ~15 lines of stdlib and it caught what a 54-section suite and two agents' review missed. Extract the section, pull every backticked lowercase identifier, resolve each against sessions.QUERY_NAMES | store.QUERY_NAMES plus the tool names regexed out of teamme_mcp.py's schemas, and allow-list the handful that are parameter names (commit_record, max_files, enabled, librarian). Before the fix it flagged recent/search/compactions; after, zero unresolved. Two design notes for whoever implements it: (1) the allow-list of parameter names must itself be derived from the tool schemas, not hardcoded, or it becomes the next second-copy-of-a-fact this repo has to fix; (2) run it over both READMEs too, not just CHANGELOG.md - the READMEs list the query tables and are equally copy-from-able.

Second live instance, same release: a false capability claim ('defaults to disabled') reached CHANGELOG.md and passed CI, because nothing checks a doc's ASSERTIONS against code - only its identifiers would be caught by the prototype above. Worth noting the honest limit of T37 as scoped: extracting backticked names catches 'this query exists', not 'this default is true'. The second class may not be mechanically checkable at all, which is an argument for the cheaper structural fix - a doc claim about a default should quote the constant's name so a reader can grep it, rather than restating its value in prose.

THIRD instance in one release entry: 'has_data: false' was documented as user-visible output when it is an internal dict key never printed. Note the pattern across all three - a query name that does not exist, a default stated backwards, and an output field the user never sees. Only the first is catchable by extracting identifiers and checking them against QUERY_NAMES. The other two need a different check, and there is a cheap one available for the third: the set of field labels a renderer actually prints is greppable from the renderer functions, so a doc claiming 'status reports X' can be checked against the strings those functions emit. Worth scoping T37 as two checks, not one: identifiers-exist (easy, high yield) and rendered-labels-exist (also mechanical).

tasks.title: Session tracking phase 2: work-completion records, cross-index queries (commit/file/task/time-range), and a cheap-model recap tier - so pre-compaction preparation is never needed
notes: USER SPEC, verbatim intent: ongoing session tracking (possibly built retroactively from past conversations) that inserts the user message, the claude message, operations pointers, AND THE FINAL DELIVERED RESPONSE once work completes - the summary naming changed files and commits, with commit details but NOT raw diffs. Purpose: scan quickly for what was done recently pre-compaction, with pointers down into raw session parts when a deeper layer is wanted. Queryable across all conversations by intake/plan/keyword/commit/file/feature/issue/time/time-range. Then a CHEAPER MODEL passes over it to generate recaps, which the librarian (a smarter model) analyses and hands to the right team agent. Goal: eliminate the pre-compaction preparation request entirely, and make frequent compaction safe even when a long context is otherwise preferred.

GROUNDED - ALREADY IMPLEMENTED in 0.6.0, so the brief must not rebuild it: turns already carry role + timestamp + text, which IS 'the user message and the claude message'. Marks already include prompt / message / answer / tool / file / compaction / recap, which IS 'operations pointers'. search_turns is the keyword axis. window IS the 'pointers to raw session parts for a deeper layer' - it fetches a bounded region around any seq. compaction already answers what fell out of context, with token counts. Subagent threads are indexed as child sessions, which matters here because on a dispatching team the delivered work happens there. So roughly half of this note describes what shipped an hour ago; the genuinely new parts are below.

GENUINELY NEW, and this is the buildable core: (1) A WORK-COMPLETION RECORD - a structured row written when a unit of work finishes, naming what was delivered, which files changed and which commits landed, with commit metadata but no diffs. No mark kind covers this today. (2) CROSS-INDEX QUERY AXES - by commit, by file, by task/intake id, by time-range. sessions stores epoch but has no between-query; history holds commits and files_changed; the worklog holds tasks. Three stores, no joins. (3) A RECAP TIER - spans summarised cheaply, stored, then read by the librarian. sessions has no equivalent of store.py's kind != 'commit' preservation, so a full reindex would destroy recaps; that seam must exist before anything writes one.

THE KEY INSIGHT, and it makes most of part 1 nearly free: THE WORK LOG IS ALREADY THE 'WHAT WAS DONE' RECORD. worklog.json has carried tasks, statuses, lanes, notes, created/updated/status_changed timestamps since day one - it is durable, committed, and survives compaction by design. The session index does NOT need to re-derive work summaries from transcript prose; it needs to LINK to the ledger that already holds them. T14's own note said this: 'the work log's own tasks, which already exist and could join to the files a task touched.' The join keys are all present: a task id appears in commit messages and in intake prose; a commit hash is in history.commits; a file path is in history.files_changed and in sessions' file marks. What is missing is the JOIN, not the data. That reframes part 1 from 'summarise work with a model' to 'record the boundary and link three existing stores' - cheaper, deterministic, and verifiable.

CONSTRAINT THAT RESHAPES THE RECAP TIER, and it is not negotiable: TEAMME'S SERVER CANNOT CALL A MODEL. Invariant #3 is stdlib python3 only, assume nothing is installed - no API client, no key, no network assumption. So 'use a cheaper model to generate recaps' cannot be a server feature. It has to be a HAIKU-TIER SUBAGENT invoked by the harness, which writes its recap back through an MCP tool - the same two-speed split phase 1 landed for history (a deterministic script extracts, a model reasons). Concretely: the server gains a WRITE tool for recap records (it has had none - every librarian tool so far is read-only except refresh), the recap agent is a second plugin-shipped agent on a small model, and the librarian reads recaps like any other row. Flag the consequence: a write tool is a new surface, and 'the librarian agents are the only callers' is convention, not enforcement - anything could write a recap. Decide whether that matters before shipping it.

HONEST DOUBT ABOUT THE GOAL, worth settling before building: the aim is 'eliminate the pre-compaction preparation request'. Indexing makes the context FETCHABLE - it does not make a future session KNOW TO FETCH IT. That gap is prompt-and-hook territory, not index territory: something has to tell the next turn 'there is a recap for this thread, read it'. The existing SessionStart hook already does exactly this shape for the work log (it surfaces unfinished tasks every session, which is why the ledger survives compaction in practice). The cheapest honest path to the stated goal may be to extend THAT - surface the most recent work-completion record and recap at SessionStart - rather than to build a deeper index and hope it gets consulted. Note the invariant: SessionStart output is additive context, never a block, so this cannot trap a session.

deferred: Spec'd, not built - the user filed this as a note. Roughly half is already shipped in 0.6.0; the new work is the work-completion record, the three-way join, and the recap tier. Start with the join, since the data already exists in three stores and needs no model.

tasks.title: Cross-index join (T38 part 2): answer 'what happened around this file / commit / task / time' across the history index, the session index and the work log
notes: GROUNDING THAT CHANGES THE DESIGN - the id-based join the note assumed does not exist in the data. Measured on this repo: commit messages cite only 3 task ids (T14, T23, T30) across 18 commits, and those are incidental prose rather than a convention; worklog notes cite only 4 distinct short SHAs. A join keyed on citation would silently return almost nothing, which is the worst outcome - an empty answer that looks like 'nothing happened' rather than 'this link was never recorded'. WHAT IS ACTUALLY RELIABLE is machine-generated on both sides: TIME (worklog created/updated/status_changed, history commit date+epoch, session turn epoch - all three stores have it, all retroactively) and FILE PATHS (history.files_changed comes from git --numstat; session 'file' marks come from observed tool calls - neither is prose). So the join is TIME-ALIGNED and FILE-ANCHORED, and any task-to-commit association is INFERENCE FROM OVERLAP, which must be labelled as such - the same 'changes with, never depends on' discipline phase 3 established.

FORWARD FIX worth proposing separately, not folding in: worklog.py could stamp 'git rev-parse HEAD' at each status transition. That turns task-to-commit from inference into an exact range (the commits between a task's start stamp and its done stamp), costs one subprocess call on a transition that already writes the file, and is a point-in-time fact rather than a copy that can drift. It does nothing retroactively, which is exactly why the time-and-file join has to exist anyway - but every task recorded after it lands would get an exact answer instead of an inferred one.

BUILT: plugins/teamme/server/librarian/cross.py - four cross-index queries (around_path, around_commit, around_task, timeline) wired into teamme_librarian_query. TIME-ALIGNED + FILE-ANCHORED as grounded, never id-based. The work log is read LIVE from .claude/intake/worklog.json on every call and joined in memory - never indexed, with the mtime-cache-not-a-copy note in a comment. ATTACH DATABASE was considered and rejected in a banner comment: either index may legitimately be absent, so one statement across both turns a missing index into a failed query instead of a partial answer that names the empty store. Ownership decision: these belong to NEITHER librarian - each store is gated separately, a disabled one removes its rows and says so, and only around_commit refuses outright (it cannot resolve its anchor hash without the history index). Every row carries store + its own address (hash / session:seq / task id) + a fetch_with. Row cap is PER STORE so 18 commits are not crowded out by 3136 turns.

VERIFIED against this repo (18 commits, 52 transcripts/3136 turns, 39 tasks), over the real MCP JSON-RPC pipe, exit 0 and empty stderr throughout. around_path(preflight.py) returned exactly the 5 commits git log reports for that file, in git's order; the worklog match returned the 6 newest of the 9 tasks that name it, correctly ordered by updated, marked TRUNCATED. around_commit(78b54d6) put the git-commit Bash call 2s before the anchor, the push 4s after and the announcement 23s after - checkable by eye. around_task(T26) surfaced the human prompt 'do T26 to close what you caought about /intake missing hook' as the spine, and the five subagent threads named in the window match the task's own notes. Degraded cases exercised on throwaway fixtures: empty project (all three stores absent, and NO directories created as a side effect), worklog-only, history-only, unparseable worklog (reads as empty, same rule as worklog.py), both librarians disabled, and nine argument/routing errors. THREE BUGS FOUND AND FIXED BY TESTING, not by reading: task rows carried no ts and rendered '(no timestamp)'; git prints the committer's UTC offset while transcripts print UTC, so a correctly epoch-sorted list READ as out of order (every row now carries a normalized ts_utc); and an unpadded task window missed the commit that closed the task by 20 seconds (pad_minutes, default 15, always reported).

Also verified the entry's '15 minutes' claim against DEFAULT_PAD_MINUTES = 15 in cross.py:112 rather than trusting it. plugin.json is 0.7.0.

tasks.title: PRIVACY DEFECT shipped in 0.6.0: the sessions index is only gitignored if teamme_librarian_configure happens to be called - refresh alone leaves conversation text un-ignored
notes: FOUND by the T39 lane while testing something else; REPRODUCED by the orchestrator before dispatching. config.apply_gitignore() has exactly ONE call site - config.py:456, inside configure(), and only when commit_record is passed. teamme_librarian_refresh never calls it. Reproduction, three commands in a fresh git repo: create .claude/librarians/sessions/index.db, run git check-ignore -> NOT IGNORED, and git status shows '?? .claude/'. THE REAL USER PATH HITS THIS DIRECTLY: both the 0.6.0 changelog and the librarian prompt tell users 'no data until the first teamme_librarian_refresh', so they run refresh, never call configure, and their conversation transcripts sit in an un-ignored file - while CLAUDE.md and both READMEs promise that directory is 'ALWAYS gitignored'. A transcript index holds everything anyone typed, including secrets pasted by accident. This is shipped on main at f907690 and a doc actively claims the opposite, which is the worst combination: a user who checks the docs is told they are safe.

FIXED in plugins/teamme/server/librarian/. New config.ensure_ignored() (enacts the CURRENT config, idempotent, never raises, creates no project dir) is called from store.ignore_guard(), wired into store.connect_file() - the single funnel every librarian index is opened through - plus append_and_insert()/rewrite_records(). Explicit calls at the top of sessions.index() and history.index() put the result in result['gitignore'] and a LOUD 'THE INDEX COULD NOT BE PROTECTED' note; the MCP refresh renderer prints it and returns isError, and no longer prints 'always gitignored' when it is not true. apply_gitignore()'s read-modify-write is now under a lock (it runs on every index open now, so two refreshes can race it). Verified with git check-ignore as ground truth: refresh-only on a fresh repo -> IGNORED; a user's pre-existing .gitignore survives byte-identical; 3 refreshes byte-identical; empty-project status still creates NOTHING (direct and over the MCP pipe); unwritable .gitignore -> refresh works and says the index is unprotected; non-git dir -> rule written anyway and said so (proved right by a non-git SUBDIR of a repo, where check-ignore confirms it protects); mangled block -> refuses and shouts; commit_record=true still leaves sessions/ ignored. Exhaustive: 504 orderings of 3 calls over 9 entry points, 952 check-ignore assertions, 0 failures - and 646 failures when the guard is disabled. SAME CLASS: history index.db had the identical hole (and commits.jsonl was un-ignored despite commit_record defaulting to false) - the same chokepoint closes both. validate.sh passes.

tasks.title: Librarian freshness gate (T14 phase 4): ask on git push when the history index is behind HEAD
notes: DESIGN: the gate is a PreToolUse hook on Bash, narrowed to git push, that returns permissionDecision "ask" - never "deny". It fires only when a history index EXISTS and is behind HEAD. No index = allow (a project that never asked for a librarian is never nagged); librarian disabled = allow; git missing, unparseable payload, unresolvable project root, marker unreadable = allow. Invariant #1 is upheld in full: every degraded state allows.

HOW THE HOOK LEARNS WHAT IS INDEXED, and why not by reading the DB: the hook is COPIED into a project (.claude/hooks/) and server/librarian/ is NOT, so it cannot import history.py. Reading the SQLite meta table from the hook would put a second copy of the schema in the copied file - the exact drift class this repo has paid for four times. Instead history.index() writes a one-line text marker .claude/librarians/history/indexed_head on every successful index, from the same place that sets META_LAST_INDEXED. One writer, one derived publication. The hook reads that line and asks git; it needs no sqlite3 and no plugin resolution.

THE LOOP BUG, pre-empted: staleness must be counted with the librarians own store excluded - git rev-list --count MARKER..HEAD -- . :!.claude/librarians - or, when commit_record is true, the commit that carries the refreshed commits.jsonl is itself unindexed and re-arms the gate that demanded it. This is invariant #2 in another costume and is the same shape as T10 (stamp against status_changed, never updated). The marker file itself joins config.ALWAYS_IGNORED (.claude/librarians/*/indexed_head) - it is machine-local derived state like the .db, and committing it is loop fuel.

SCOPE: history only. The sessions librarian has no notion of being behind HEAD and is not consulted by this gate - say so in the docs rather than leaving a reader to wonder. Also: adding a hook script grows REQUIRED_HOOKS, so every existing install becomes installed-outdated on upgrade and is told to run /teamme:team-doctor, never /teamme:init-team. That is the designed path T23 paid a P0 for; the release notes must say it plainly.

hook-engineer: shipped the gate. history.py writes .claude/librarians/history/indexed_head atomically beside the META_LAST_INDEXED write (one writer); a failed marker write leaves ok=true plus marker_published=false and a note. config.py: MARKER_IGNORE .claude/librarians/*/indexed_head added to ALWAYS_IGNORED - verified protected at store.connect_file() -> ignore_guard -> config.ensure_ignored, with git check-ignore as ground truth. New templates/hooks/librarian-gate.py: PreToolUse/Bash, ask-only, silent on non-push, no index, disabled librarian, bad/unreachable marker, git missing, 4s git timeout, malformed payload. Count excludes ':!.claude/librarians' - measured: without it the commit carrying a refreshed commits.jsonl counts 1 and re-arms the gate forever; with it, 0. Registered as a second PreToolUse group; added to REQUIRED_HOOKS (missing = installed-outdated, 7/7); teamme_librarian_status now reports the marker and a marker/index divergence. validate.sh passes (no new assertions - validation lane next).

HOOK LANE LANDED. New templates/hooks/librarian-gate.py; marker written by history.index() beside the META_LAST_INDEXED set; MARKER_IGNORE joins ALWAYS_IGNORED; second PreToolUse group (matcher Bash); REQUIRED_HOOKS now 7; teamme_mcp status prints a three-way marker line including MARKER DIVERGED. Verified independently by me: exactly one "deny" in the hook (a docstring sentence), all 7 template/copy pairs byte-identical, the pathspec exclusion present with its reasoning at the call site. THE LOOP WAS MEASURED, NOT ARGUED: with commit_record=true, rev-list at the same marker returns 1 without the exclusion and 0 with it. _check_settings needed no change - it asserts REQUIRED_EVENTS has a truthy entry, never matchers, so a second PreToolUse group needs no list to grow.

PROMPT LANE LANDED. init-team.md names librarian-gate.py in the copy-verbatim list (invariant #5) and the shared guardrail block now tells team agents what to do when they MEET the ask - consult history-librarian, which refreshes - because team agents have no librarian tools and editing .claude/librarians/ to quiet a prompt is never the answer. team-doctor.md gained a "My push started asking me something" section. history-librarian.md now owns the stale-index contract: a librarian answering from an index behind HEAD says so IN the answer, plus a three-row table for the indexed_head line and a refusal bullet saying it cannot silence the reminder. templates/intake.md deliberately UNCHANGED - the contract is owned by the librarian prompt and restating it there would be a second copy of a fact owned elsewhere, in the one file that gets worse with every added line. Verified by me: frontmatter parses on all five prompt files, no FORBIDDEN_AGENT_KEYS.

tasks.title: store.ignore_guard imports config without a loose-module fallback, so a loose import silently skips the gitignore protection
notes: Found by the hook lane while VERIFYING the connect_file -> ignore_guard -> ensure_ignored chain for T41, not by inspection. Every other cross-module import under server/librarian/ carries an except ImportError loose fallback; ignore_guard does "from . import config" with none. Import store as a loose module (sys.path.insert on server/librarian, then import store) and the ImportError is swallowed into a problem dict nobody inspects at connect_file - no .gitignore written, no error surfaced. NOT a live defect: both real callers import it as a package (teamme_mcp.py via importlib.import_module("librarian.store"), validate.sh via "from librarian import store"), so neither production nor CI reaches it. The hazard is that the one code path carrying the privacy guarantee is also the one that degrades silently under an import style the rest of the package tolerates. Fix is one except ImportError away; the harder question is whether a swallowed problem dict at connect_file should be silent at all.

Fixed: ignore_guard now uses the same try-package/except-ImportError-loose fallback every other cross-module import in server/librarian uses. Also changed the silence: a failed guard is recorded in store._UNPROTECTED (bounded at 8, deduped) and drained by teamme_mcp.with_protection_report, which appends an UNPROTECTED block to every librarian tool result, so a query that opens an unprotected index now says so. It only adds text, never changes isError, never raises - protection failing still cannot stop the work.

FIXED, and the lane went past the one-liner as invited. (1) ignore_guard now carries the same try/except ImportError loose fallback the rest of the package uses - the defect was first REPRODUCED (loose import -> problem dict, no .gitignore written) and then re-run after the fix (ok, and git check-ignore confirms both index paths ignored). (2) The silence changed: store.py gained note_unprotected/take_unprotected over a capped, deduped module-level list, and teamme_mcp.py wraps all four librarian tools in with_protection_report, which APPENDS an UNPROTECTED block and never sets isError, never raises, and cannot stop an index opening. Previously only the refresh paths reported their own ensure_ignored result, so a QUERY opening an unprotected index said nothing at all. It suppresses itself when the result already contains UNPROTECTED so a refresh still renders only its own fuller block, and drains the record either way so a failure is reported on the call it happened on and never repeated stale.

tasks.title: The intake.md install-evidence probe keys on mere existence but reports 'was generated here' - a stranger's repo with its own intake.md is misread as a teamme install
notes: Found while asserting the roster check (T3), reasoned away by the docs lane as an already-documented consequence of evidence-based existence. It is not. preflight.py _install_evidence() does: if (root/".claude"/"commands"/"intake.md").is_file(): reasons.append(".claude/commands/intake.md was generated here") - the probe tests EXISTENCE and the reason string claims GENERATION, which the probe cannot know. "intake" is not a teamme-only word, so a project with its own hand-written .claude/commands/intake.md is reported as evidence teamme was installed there.

Consequence: that project gets installed-outdated rather than not-installed, and is told to REPAIR - which writes teamme scaffolding into a repo that never asked for it - instead of being told to install. The mirror image of the T23 P0: T23 told installed users they were not installed and pointed them at a destructive reinstall; this tells never-installed users they ARE installed and points them at a write. Milder (it needs an unrelated intake.md to exist, and the repair asks first), hence P1 not P0. Note also that CLAUDE.md-s validate.sh no-false-positive assertion covers the HOOKS probe only - a stranger-s repo carrying an unrelated SessionStart hook - and there is no equivalent fixture for the intake.md probe. The Decisions-already-made entry also says "a GENERATED .claude/commands/intake.md", which is the same over-claim as the reason string.
